extracted.intended_audience: readers and communicators (public figures, PR professionals, journalists) interested in crafting or evaluating public apologies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for composing and judging public apologies—what elements make an apology authentic, how drafts succeed or fail, and how to repair harm publicly. Uses Dan Harmon/Megan Ganz as a case study to illustrate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate that the accusation or criticism has been taken seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that the accusation or criticism has been taken seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the first necessary component in the post's 'Rubric Review' — the apologizer must show they have actually listened to and considered the complaint (not merely issued a perfunctory statement). Examples in the post contrast vague, dismissive drafts with later drafts that directly address the harmed person's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a statement of accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a statement of accountability (something akin to “I’m sorry.”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit admission of responsibility — not deflection or euphemism. The post emphasizes clear 'I' language rather than passive or distancing phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a commitment to personal growth and/or repairing the harm caused
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a commitment to personal growth and/or repairing the harm caused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The apology should promise and indicate concrete steps toward change or repair (not only expression of regret). The post scores apologies by whether they show evidence of future-oriented repair or growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology grading scale (scoring guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An excellent apology (A+ to A-) will show evidence of all three components. Less stellar apologies (B+ to C-) may include one or two. An apology fails (D+ to D-) if it does not include any of these components or undermines any of these components at any point in the apology. A student who does not complete the assignment (i.e., doesn’t offer an apology when one is warranted) receives an F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence of the three core components to map to grades. Also consider whether components are undermined later in the apology (which can downgrade the evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity about actions and harms (allocution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific about what you did and how it harmed the person(s) — 'Redemption follows allocution' and Ganz asked Harmon to be more specific about his behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague statements ('sorry for being a bad boss') are inadequate; name concrete behaviors, timeframes, and impacts. The post cites Megan Ganz's demand for specificity and her detailed notes as crucial to making Harmon’s apology credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using cluelessness/ignorance as cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not hide behind 'I didn't know' or claims of cluelessness as a way to diminish responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post criticizes drafts that couch wrongdoing in deferred realizations ('I didn't know I was doing it when I did it') because that reduces accountability. An authentic apology acknowledges that ignorance is not a full excuse and avoids framing the apology as discovery rather than ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full ownership with explicit 'I' statements and acknowledgement of consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit ownership language (many 'I' statements) and acknowledge the concrete consequences of your actions (e.g., lost job, damaged career, harmed internal compass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post praises Harmon’s later draft for listing cascading consequences and accepting responsibility for them; such explicit ownership increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer repair and relief to the harmed person (invite and act on what would help)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a commitment to repair harm and, where appropriate, ask the harmed person what would give them relief ('Figure out how to give me that relief and I'll return the favor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repair can include concrete actions, restitution, facilitating the harmed person's recovery of career/confidence, and following the harmed person's instructions about what would help. The post highlights Ganz asking Harmon to 'figure out how to give me that relief' as an important reparative framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicness and transparency when harm is public
rubrics_metrics.description: When wrongdoing and its effects are public, the apology and forgiveness process may need to be public as well ('this was never about vengeance; it’s about vindication... it didn’t feel right to just accept his apology in private').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that Ganz preferred a public apology and that doing restorative work 'in the light' matters for public harms; consider audience and whether private apologies suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with and listen to the harmed person; incorporate their feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage the harmed person, listen to their account, and incorporate their feedback into the apology (Ganz provided detailed notes and edited Harmon’s draft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The collaborative editing between victim and apologizer is presented as rare but powerful; meaningful engagement can transform a vague confession into a credible apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apology from confession/self-defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting the apology function primarily as a confession or self-defense; an apology should not be a vehicle for justifying or minimizing one's actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post characterizes some early drafts as confessions wrapped in self-defense. A genuine apology centers the harmed person's experience rather than the apologizer's rationalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate reflection and higher-order thinking about choices ('not thinking' vs 'not knowing')
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that you have reflected on your choices (the difference between 'not knowing' and 'not thinking about it') and that you will consciously choose better in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post praises Harmon for articulating that he 'did it by not thinking about it' — an admission that he failed to reflect and a pledge to change that mode of operation is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your platform to invite broader change and encourage others to think/act differently
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a public platform, use it to call others to reflection and cultural change (e.g., Harmon’s call to audience: 'Think about it... we can make it a normal part of our culture that we think about it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An apology that leverages influence to prevent similar harms and promote discussion and policy/cultural shifts is evaluated more positively in the post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and proactivity: voluntary apology vs only after public pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Apologizing without being prompted (proactive contrition) is evidence of willingness to reexamine and account for past behavior; apologies issued only after public pressure may be weaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post awards some credit when Harmon reexamined behavior and apologized publicly before direct confrontation, though it also critiques tardy or insufficient drafts. Consider whether the apology was voluntary and timely.
